idiom_name: opaque handle typedef + create/destroy/user function cluster
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the pattern is hand-written: declare an incomplete struct in the public header (typedef struct ringbuffer ringbuffer_t;), define that struct only in the implementation file, and expose functions that take the handle as their first argument. The create and destroy functions play the constructor/destructor role and are the only places that allocate and release the resource; the remaining functions coalesce a raw group of calls (open/read/write/close) into intent-named operations and return an error code instead of an errno the caller must remember to check (see CERT DCL12-C). Because there is no destructor, the wrapper must offer exactly one obvious teardown path and document that the handle it returns is owned by the caller until then.
pitfalls: Nothing enforces the call order: a NULL handle, a double destroy or a use-after-destroy is a runtime bug, so every function must validate its handle and the header must document who owns it.
Defining the struct in the public header silently removes the encapsulation and lets callers poke at the fields, after which the implementation can never change.
With no destructor, the create/destroy pairing is easy to skip on early-return and error paths; goto-style cleanup or an explicit scope helper is the usual mitigation.
errno is a per-thread convention the wrapper must capture immediately: a facade that defers the check can report the wrong error.
